who: Derek Stanley Chang, historian at Cornell University; PhD Duke University, 2002.

evidence.says: Cornell lists Derek Chang as an associate professor of history researching American social and religious history.
The dissertation list names Derek Stanley Chang and his Duke University dissertation, Breaking the Shackles of Hierarchy, completed in 2002.
The authority for Derek Chang was established from Breaking the shackles of hierarchy (2002), the matching dissertation.
The other exact-name candidate is associated with a 2022 workplace infection-modeling report and the U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center.

notes: The dissertation title, university, year and field identify no2002105351. The second exact-name authority concerns a different researcher.

who: Thomas M. Coakley, historian of Tudor-Stuart England at Miami University, 1963–1993; PhD University of Minnesota.

evidence.says: The retirement notice on page 6 identifies Thomas M. Coakley, his Minnesota doctorate on Robert Cecil, and his Miami teaching from 1963 to 1993.
This candidate is Thomas P. Coakley, author of C3I in real life (1991), rather than Thomas M. Coakley.
This candidate is Thomas Francis Coakley, author of Catholic doctrines in the Protestant Bible (1940); the authority chronology precedes the supervisor’s Miami career.
This candidate is Tom Coakley, established from the sound recording An evening with Tom Coakley and his Orchestra.

notes: None of the three authorities identifies the Miami historian Thomas M. Coakley.

who: Arlene J. Díaz, Latin American historian at Indiana University Bloomington; PhD University of Minnesota, 1997.

evidence.says: Indiana identifies Arlene Díaz as history faculty, lists her Minnesota PhD in 1997, and includes her article on gender conflicts in early republican Caracas.

The 1998 article credits Arlene J. Díaz. Its author note identifies her as Indiana University Bloomington history faculty working on Ciudadanas and padres de familia, a manuscript about gender, power and law in Caracas.
The authority identifies Arlene J. Diaz as author of Ciudadanas and padres de familia (1994).

notes: The full author name, Caracas research and related manuscript title connect this authority to the Indiana faculty member; her doctorate also matches.

who: Arthur Benoit (Ben) Eklof, historian of Russia at Indiana University from 1977; PhD history, Princeton University, 1977.

evidence.says: His April 2018 CV gives his full name as Arthur Benoit Eklof, a Princeton history PhD in 1977, and successive Indiana history appointments beginning in 1977.
This candidate is Anders Eklöf, author of Project work, independence and critical thinking (2014), affiliated with Kristianstad University.
This candidate is August Eklöf, a historical subject of L. Heiman’s Kaksi kauppaneuvosta (1980), rather than an authority for Ben Eklof.

notes: Both candidates have different full names and identities. Neither is Arthur Benoit Eklof.

who: George Frederick Frick, historian of early American botany and science at the University of Delaware; PhD University of Illinois.

evidence.says: Edward Lurie’s obituary identifies George F. Frick as a Delaware history faculty member for 31 years, with an Illinois doctorate and publications on naturalist Mark Catesby.
The George Frederick Frick authority cites Mark Catesby: the colonial Audubon (1961) and Mark Catesby, naturalist, 1683–1749 (1958).

notes: The distinctive Catesby works connect the fuller authority name to the Delaware historian; the institution, period and doctoral university agree.

who: Wesley Marsh Gewehr, University of Maryland history professor and department head from 1940; PhD University of Chicago, 1922.

evidence.says: Clio at College Park, chapter II, identifies Wesley M. Gewehr as Maryland’s history professor and department head from 1940, educated at Chicago, and author of The Great Awakening in Virginia.
The university library’s index records a July 1922 announcement that Wesley M. Gewehr received his doctorate from Chicago.
The authority expands Wesley M. Gewehr to Wesley Marsh Gewehr and cites The Great Awakening in Virginia.

notes: Full name, distinctive book, Maryland appointment and Chicago doctorate agree.

who: William D. Gilliam, historian supervising at the University of Kentucky; PhD Indiana University, 1941.

evidence.says: Western Kentucky University’s finding aid identifies William D. Gilliam as author of The Public Career of Robert Perkins Letcher, an Indiana University doctoral thesis submitted in 1941.
This authority was established from a Camden County Historical Society deed dated 1869, identifying a nineteenth-century William Gilliam.
This authority concerns the subject of the archival collection William Gilliam Papers, circa 1850s–1890s, rather than the twentieth-century historian.
The remaining authority is W. Craig Gilliam, author of time for change?: revisioning your call (2000).

W. Craig Gilliam’s professional biography describes organizational consulting and industrial/organizational psychology, including teaching at SMU and a dissertation on leadership, anxiety and organizational conflict.

notes: The AHA doctoral school and year correspond to William D. Gilliam. The two historical authorities and W. Craig Gilliam are different people.

who: John Edmond Gonzales, historian of the nineteenth-century South at the University of Southern Mississippi; PhD University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill.

evidence.says: Senate Resolution 41 identifies John Edmond Gonzales as a longtime Southern Mississippi history professor with a UNC Chapel Hill doctorate, specializing in nineteenth-century southern history and editing the Journal of Mississippi History.
The university names Dr. John Gonzales among the history faculty directing its original oral history program in spring 1971.
The authority cites A Mississippi reader (1980), identifying John Edmond Gonzales as a Southern Mississippi history professor and editor of the Journal of Mississippi History.

notes: Full name, university, field, doctoral institution and journal editorship agree; university evidence places him there during the students’ period.
